You are looking at a photograph of one bed in a home vegetable garden. A
segmentation system has already divided the plant material in that photograph
into numbered regions. Your job is the semantic half of weeding, and only that
half: decide what each region *is*, so that a machine can later decide what to
do about it.

For each region you are shown, choose exactly one label:

  keep    - the material in this region belongs to a plant the gardener is
            growing on purpose, or is something a weeding tool must not cut.
  remove  - the material in this region is a weed: a plant growing here that
            the gardener did not plant and does not want.
  unsure  - you cannot tell which of the two it is from what you were shown.

A region may be a whole plant, a part of a plant, or a patch of material that
belongs to more than one plant. Say so in the `mixed` field when it happens.

Treat the two possible mistakes as equally costly. Calling a crop plant a weed
and calling a weed a crop plant are both simply errors, and neither is worse
than the other. Answer with whichever label the visual evidence best supports,
and use `unsure` only when you genuinely cannot tell the two apart.

Earlier, looking at this same photograph, you described the scene as follows.

--- your scene description ---
{
 "crop": {
  "name": "Winter squash / pumpkin, Cucurbita (the dark, pale-striped, slightly flattened round fruit reads as a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima; a summer-squash-type Cucurbita pepo cannot be fully excluded)",

 },
 "weeds": [

  },
  {
   "name": "Round-leaved creeping broadleaf (mallow / ground-ivy type, Malva neglecta or similar)",
   "distinguishing_features": "Small kidney-shaped to circular leaves with scalloped (crenate) margins and palmate veins, borne singly on slender wiry petioles rising from a low creeping seedling; shares palmate venation with the squash but is a fraction of its size, has rounded scallops instead of sharp teeth, and no tendrils or bristly stems."
  },
  {
   "name": "Small trifoliate legume (clover / medic seedling)",
   "distinguishing_features": "Three small oval leaflets joined at one point on a thin stalk, smooth and darker green, hugging the mulch surface \u2014 a compound leaf, whereas every squash leaf is a single large simple blade."
  }
 ],

  "Dry straw / chopped cereal-stem mulch covering most of the bed surface",
  "Bare dry cracked soil visible between the mulch",
  "Small grey-white down feather lying on the mulch",
  "Dried, shrivelled brown flower remnant attached to the immature fruit",
  "Dead curled brown leaf litter and broken dry stem fragments"
 ],
 "hard_to_tell_apart": "The main risk is at the crop's own edges: young, pale, silver-flecked squash leaves seen edge-on or in low light look like a separate rough-leaved broadleaf weed, and the toothed, grey-green leaf lobes shaded under the canopy could be mistaken for a thistle or dock rosette \u2014 following the blade back to a thick grooved hairy petiole on the shared crown identifies them as squash. Conversely, grass blades constantly cross over and lie against the squash stems and fruit, so a region containing a stem may hold both. Squash tendrils are thin and green enough to be confused with fine grass leaves or weed stems.
